also: what do you do for a living?
what line of work are you in?

terms.gloss: What is your job, your post?
evidence: Plin. Ep. 3.5.9: inde ad dēlēgātum sibi officium
terms.comment: As Latin speakers ask it today. Officium is properly a duty or a service; from Caesar on it is also an official post or employment (Lewis & Short), as when the elder Pliny goes off before dawn to the post assigned him. Of any job at all, the use is modern. The answer is the plain noun: Medicus sum.

terms.gloss: What post do you hold? What is your work?
terms.grammar: fungor, fungī, fūnctus sum with the ablative
evidence: Plin. Ep. 7.19.2: Quō mūnere Fannia dum sēdulō fungitur
terms.comment: Mūnus is a post, an office, one’s function (Lewis & Short: “a service, office, post, employment”), and mūnere fungī the classical phrase for doing it. The question itself is ours on that phrase; Latin speakers today ask it so too.

terms.gloss: What trade or profession do you practise?
evidence: Hor. Ep. 1.14.44: quam scit uterque, libēns, cēnsēbō, exerceat artem
terms.comment: Of a trade or a profession as a skill (ars); see “profession”.
Traupman’s question. Take care: in Plautus and Terence quaestum facere by itself is said of a prostitute (Lewis & Short s.v. quaestus).

phrases.latin: Quod est officium tuum? — Programmātor sum.
phrases.english: What’s your job? — I’m a programmer.

phrases.latin: Quō mūnere pater tuus fungitur? — Medicus est.
phrases.english: What does your father do? — He’s a doctor.

phrases.latin: Quō mūnere Fannia dum sēdulō fungitur, hōc discrīmine implicita est.
phrases.english: While Fannia was carefully doing this duty, she caught this dangerous illness.

phrases.latin: Optat ephippia bōs piger, optat arāre caballus; quam scit uterque, libēns, cēnsēbō, exerceat artem.
phrases.english: The lazy ox wants a saddle, the horse wants to plough; my verdict will be that each should gladly ply the trade he knows.
